newsitem.title: UK: Eurosceptic Redwood bids to lead UK Conservatives.
newsitem.headline: Eurosceptic Redwood bids to lead UK Conservatives.

text.p: Hardline Eurosceptic John Redwood joined the battle for the leadership of Britain's dispirited Conservatives on Tuesday, denying that the party would be split if he was chosen for the "awesome" task.

Redwood, the third member of parliament to declare he would bid to replace John Major, said the fact that he had been outside Major's cabinet for two years before Thursday's election defeat by the Labour Party would be to his advantage.

Major announced he would step down as party leader after the Conservatives' election debacle last Thursday, when they won just 156 of the 659 seats in the House of Commons, their worst showing for 150 years.
Kenneth Clarke, the pro-European former Finance Minister, and right-winger Peter Lilley have already put themselves forward as the men to lead the party out of the wilderness.
Former Interior Minister Michael Howard has called a news conference for 1430 GMT at which he too is expected to throw his hat into the ring.

These three are more in the Conservative mainstream than Redwood, who challenged Major for the party leadership in 1995 on a programme demanding that British membership of the European Union single currency be ruled out.
But Redwood played the unity card on Tuesday. "I don't want a sectional party, a factional party, a party obsessed by only one issue," he told a news conference.
"I believe the Conservative Party is a broad church. It must stay a broad church. The trouble is we don't have enough worshippers at the moment."

Redwood, 45, said he was well placed to provide leadership for the fight-back because he had been out of ministerial office for two years before the election -- he resigned as Welsh Secretary in 1995 to challenge Major.
"Against (Prime Minister) Tony Blair across the despatch box, I would not have to defend every last deed of the 1992-7 government, and could look forward," he said.
In the 1995 contest, Redwood was well beaten by Major, who has led the party since replacing Margaret Thatcher in 1990.
After his defeat, Redwood formed a right-wing think-tank and, although not openly attacking Major, continued to put forward his Eurosceptic views widely and openly.
In a BBC radio interview, Redwood said it should now be possible for him and Clarke, on the opposite wings of the party on the European issue, to unite.
"Ken and I are...entirely united in saying that a fudged single currrency will not work and would be bad for Britain. I don't think there will be anything other than a fudged one on offer," he said.

Former Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine has ruled himself out of the race because of ill health, and the bookmakers William Hill make William Hague, who replaced Redwood as Welsh Secretary, the favourite to replace Major.
Hague, a right-winger who is just 36, has yet to say whether he will stand but is still quoted at 6-4, while Clarke is second favourite at 4-1 and Redwood is on 10-1.
